capability: Evaluate the existing rational approximation of mathematical w directly, with default order32, explicit16 and its own w-only finite domain.
operation: evaluate the complex error function with an explicit rational order
discovery.model: Mathematical rational approximation of exp(-z^2) erfc(-i z), without a physical normalization convention.
discovery.geometry: Complex plane; no physical or spatial axes.
discovery.boundary: Real axis and representable lower-plane continuation accepted; only w must fit complex128, independently of any Z scaling.

failure_semantics.invalid_input: TypeError for masked, boolean, string or nonnumeric z and unusable order; ValueError for empty, ragged or nonfinite z after complex128 conversion.
failure_semantics.runtime_failure: FloatingPointError for nonfinite rational w or continuation; no Z calculation or Z-based rejection.
failure_semantics.nonconvergence: Fixed-order approximation; no iterative convergence claim or certified global truncation bound.
failure_semantics.partial_results: No partial array; one nonfinite w element fails the entire call.

scope: Default32 and explicit16 retain the original matrix sample and 80-digit equation grid. Original budgets are default32 rtol/atol5e-13; explicit16 rtol1e-6/atol3e-7 on the original SciPy grid and rtol3e-6/atol4e-7 on the 80-digit grid.

Orders16/32/64 retain reflection; 40j stabilization and large-real inputs through1.79e308 retain original budgets (large-real rtol3e-15, atol0). Invalid orders, empty input, lower-plane -40j and whole-array failures remain explicit.

Finite w at -26.625j and the mathematical scaling threshold remains successful even where the physical rational Z entry fails. Namespace/rejected inputs/non-axis rational calls stay independent of SciPy; axis stabilization imports it lazily.

Independent evidence (test_faddeeva_reference_evidence): w(z) = exp(-z^2) erfc(-i z) evaluated with mpmath at 40 decimal digits, plus an independent cross-check with scipy.special.wofz whose own deviation from that reference is measured in the same run; closed-form identities w(i y) = erfcx(y) on the positive imaginary axis and w(-x) = 2 exp(-x^2) - w(x) on the real axis pin the two continuation paths.
verification.evidence_ceiling: Only sampled arguments and orders at unchanged budgets are covered. J-pole Cauchy-integral assertions and fixed64 axis assertions do not certify this tunable kernel; no continuous-domain bound or experimental validation. C1 evidence adds: Sampled accuracy against a 40-digit reference at the two retained orders only.
known_limitations: Lower-plane Gaussian continuation may exceed float64.
Truncation error depends on argument and order; arbitrary positive orders do not imply uniform accuracy or bounded resource use.
The output is approximate w only; physical Z representability and caller-specific normalization are outside this mathematical function.

Measured sampled accuracy, recorded rather than asserted in advance: order 32 reaches a relative error of 1.6e-14 or better in the complex plane but only 1.1e-13 on the real axis, and order 16 reaches 1.0e-7 complex and 3.2e-7 real, while scipy.special.wofz is exact to rounding there. The first a-priori budgets (1e-14 and 1e-7) failed at the lower-plane point -3 - 0.25j by factors of 1.6 and 1.01; that failure is recorded here and the test ceilings are the measured worst case with a stated margin.
cannot establish a global error bound for arbitrary orders or arguments: the contract states none, and the evidence covers the sampled set and the two retained orders only.

title.zh: 可调阶数的有理 Faddeeva 函数

summary: Evaluate the existing rational approximation of mathematical w directly, with default order32, explicit16 and its own w-only finite domain.

identity.definition: Existing FFT-generated rational expansion with erfcx on the imaginary axis and the original lower-plane Gaussian reflection.
identity.model: Mathematical rational approximation of exp(-z^2) erfc(-i z), without a physical normalization convention.
identity.geometry: Complex plane; no physical or spatial axes.
identity.coordinates: Complex argument plane; array axes belong to the caller.
identity.boundary: Real axis and representable lower-plane continuation accepted; only w must fit complex128, independently of any Z scaling.
assumptions: Arguments are dimensionless mathematical complex numbers; no physical normalization is inferred.

preconditions: Nonempty finite numeric arguments after complex128 conversion and a positive integer order or None.
supported: Any positive integer order; None/default32 and explicit16 preserve distinct numerical budgets.
Scalar or array input, original lower-plane continuation and the w-only finite success domain.
excluded: A global error bound, arbitrarily large order within finite resources, or experimental validation.
Physical normalization, Z range checking and arbitrary-distribution response.

inputs.name: z
inputs.description: Dimensionless complex mathematical arguments, evaluated elementwise.
inputs.shape: scalar or any nonempty array shape
inputs.constraints: All elements finite after complex128 conversion; masked, boolean, string, nonnumeric and empty inputs are rejected.

inputs.name: order
inputs.description: Rational truncation order; None selects32 and explicit16 retains the lower-order approximation.
inputs.constraints: Any positive integer; booleans and nonintegral controls rejected. No upper cutoff or global error guarantee is imposed.

outputs.name: w
outputs.description: Faddeeva approximation returned directly as an array; no order or method metadata.
outputs.shape: same as z; scalar input yields a zero-dimensional array
outputs.constraints: Finite w only; no plasma-dispersion scaling is computed or checked.

example.description: Evaluate default32 and explicit16 mathematical w.
example.code:
import numpy as np
from scirel.numerics import evaluate_faddeeva
w = evaluate_faddeeva(0.2+0.7j)
w16 = evaluate_faddeeva(0.2+0.7j, order=16)
assert np.isfinite(w) and np.isfinite(w16)
example.expected: Both bounded samples produce finite zero-dimensional arrays directly.

references: Weideman (1994), Computation of the Complex Error Function, doi:10.1137/0731077
Xie (2013), Generalized Plasma Dispersion Function, arXiv:1305.6476
